question: What were the main findings of WHO's World Malaria Report 2024?
seconds_estimate: ~8-12s (Researched 1s badge; streaming completed within ~10s of submit)
answer_inline_citations_format: Perplexity shows source-site chips (e.g. 'who +2', 'cdn.who +1', 'repository.gheli.harvard') rather than numeric markers. The +N means N additional sources beyond the one shown.
answer:
The World Malaria Report 2024, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in December 2024, presents a mixed picture: while billions of cases and millions of deaths have been averted since 2000, global progress toward malaria targets is off track, with rising case numbers and persistent inequities. [who +2]

Global burden in 2023

In 2023, there were an estimated 263 million malaria cases worldwide—about 11 million more than in 2022. [who +2]

Malaria caused an estimated 597,000 deaths globally in 2023. [who +1]

The WHO African Region bore the overwhelming burden: roughly 94% of cases and 95% of deaths. [who +1]

Since 2000, an estimated 2.2 billion cases and 12.7 million deaths have been averted globally due to malaria control efforts. [who +1]

Progress toward global targets

Current trends are not on pace to meet key global malaria targets for 2030. [cdn.who +1]

The 2023 global malaria incidence rate was 60.4 cases per 1,000 population at risk, nearly three times higher than the 2030 target of 21.3. [who]

The malaria mortality rate in 2023 was 13.7 deaths per 100,000 at-risk population, more than double the 2030 target of 5.5. [who]

As of December 2024, 44 countries and one territory have been certified malaria-free by WHO, with many more progressing toward elimination. [cdn.who]

Key drivers of stalled progress

The report identifies several systemic and emerging challenges:

Fragile health systems and weak surveillance limit timely detection and response. [cdn.who +1]

Funding gaps constrain scale-up of proven interventions. [cdn.who +1]

Drug and insecticide resistance are rising threats undermining control tools. [cdn.who +1]

Climate change, conflict, displacement, and natural disasters are exacerbating vulnerability and disrupting services. [cdn.who]

Many high-risk and marginalized populations still lack access to prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. [who +1]

Promising interventions and scale-up

Despite challenges, the report highlights important gains in prevention:

Expanded use of new-generation insecticide-treated nets (including dual-ingredient nets). [cdn.who]

Rollout of WHO-recommended malaria vaccines (RTS,S and R21/Matrix-M) in more countries. [cdn.who +1]

Growth in seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), reaching tens of millions of children in high-transmission areas. [cdn.who +1]

In 2023 alone, these and other measures are estimated to have averted more than 177 million cases and 1 million deaths globally. [who]

Equity as a central theme

For the first time, the 2024 report includes a dedicated chapter on equity, urging a more inclusive response that reaches the most vulnerable. It calls for addressing inequities linked to: [who +1]

Gender, socioeconomic status, disability, ethnicity, and migrant status. [repository.gheli.harvard]

Geographic and systemic barriers in fragile and conflict-affected settings. [cdn.who +1]

The overarching message is that accelerating progress will require stronger health systems, sustained financing, innovation to counter resistance, and a deliberate focus on leaving no one behind. [cdn.who +1]
